children.text: No — when gated correctly, zero React reaches published visitors. This is provable from the wrapper's source: the entire @sanity/astro <VisualEditing/> component is a conditional island render.
Three caveats make the claim precise:
enabled={false} means zero React reaches the visitor.

The island is never rendered: no <astro-island> marker, no chunk request, no React runtime download. Astro only loads a framework renderer for islands actually on the page, so react() in the config costs published pages nothing. The ~690 kB visual-editing chunk is still emitted to the build output — it sits on the CDN unused — but emitted-to-dist and shipped-to-browsers are different things.
The gate is your responsibility.

“Never ships” is only as true as whatever you pass to enabled. Wired correctly (per-request preview: enabled={Astro.locals.preview}), visitors get nothing; wired wrong, every visitor downloads ~228 kB gzipped of React + overlay renderer. Nothing in the package enforces the gate.
“Enabled” is not “active”.

Once enabled={true}, client:only="react" loads the chunk on page load — immediately, whether or not the page is inside the Presentation tool. In an env-flag deployment model, an entire preview site ships React to anyone who reaches it; with per-request gating, only validated editors trigger it. The same nuance applies to the vanilla path: enableVisualEditing() kicks off the lazy renderer chunk (also React internally) as soon as the script runs, not when the Studio connects.

So the fair summary: the React integration's runtime cost to end users is zero when gated correctly — the objection to it was never bundle size on published pages. The legitimate objections are the ones that remain regardless: @astrojs/react, react and react-dom in your dependency tree and toolchain (peer-dep installs, version management, one more renderer in the build), and the on-principle oddity of a framework-agnostic platform's first-party integration mandating a specific framework for a feature that — as this site demonstrates — does not need it.

question: If we do use the React integration, does React ever ship to the published site?

children.text: They can set the cookie, but not to a value the server accepts. The cookie name is public — names never matter — but the accepted value is an HMAC keyed by the server-only read token:
Forging it without the key is a 2²⁵⁶ brute force — and anyone who already has the token does not need the cookie; they could query drafts directly. We verified a hand-set
sanity-preview=true
still gets published content.

The realistic vectors are theft, not forgery: the value is static and never expires, so treat it like a secret. httpOnly blocks XSS reads, production must use HTTPS with secure cookies, and rotating the token instantly invalidates every issued cookie. If stolen, the blast radius is read access to drafts — no write access, and the HMAC does not reverse to the token. Hardening option: embed a signed expiry in the value and compare with timingSafeEqual.

question: Can someone spoof the preview cookie?

children.text: Almost none — and this is verifiable from the package's type definitions rather than docs. The React component's props type is literally
VisualEditingOptions & { portal: boolean }
— the exact same options object that enableVisualEditing() takes, plus one React-only prop. The component is the function with lifecycle management around it.
Identical in both

(it is the same core overlay controller): click-to-edit overlays, stega element resolution, the Presentation comlink handshake, drag-and-drop array reordering, context menus, URL/history sync (history adapter), zIndex, refresh, keepStegaOnCopy, onPerspectiveChange, onVariantChange, onSuspiciousStega, and even the alpha plugins/components overlay-customization options. The default refresh in both is location.reload().
What vanilla actually loses:
Automatic lifecycle.

The component calls the function on mount and the returned DisableVisualEditing cleanup on unmount; vanilla hands you that disable function to manage yourself. Moot for a full-page-load MPA like this site; with Astro View Transitions, re-run enableVisualEditing() on astro:after-swap (~three lines).
The portal prop.
A React-only choice about whether overlays render inside your component tree or an appended DOM node. Meaningless outside React.
The React hooks that live next to the component

(the real functional gap — and it belongs to the /react entry, not the component): useOptimistic and useDocuments (in-place optimistic UI during drag-reorder, so the preview updates before the mutation round-trips), useIsPresentationTool and useVisualEditingEnvironment (e.g. show a “disable draft mode” button only outside Presentation), and the alpha usePresentationQuery (block-level re-fetching for lower-latency editing of heavy pages). These are React state integrations — there is no vanilla equivalent because there is no React state to integrate with. Edits still appear; they arrive via your refresh handler instead of patching the UI in place.
One caveat on overlay customization.

The alpha components/plugins option is available in vanilla, but the custom overlay components you would author for it are typed as React components (the overlay renderer is React internally) — so customizing the overlay UI itself means writing React either way.

For an SSR Astro (+ Svelte) site the practical difference is exactly one thing: edit-latency during preview. The React ecosystem gets in-place optimistic updates; vanilla gets refresh-driven updates (reload, or smarter logic in your refresh handler). Everything an editor sees — overlays, click-to-edit, drag-reorder, Presentation navigation — is identical, because it all lives in the framework-agnostic core. This very page is the empirical proof: fully editable in Presentation with zero React in the frontend.

children.text: @sanity/astro
. The changelog entry is explicit: “⚠ BREAKING CHANGES — This deprecates the useSanityClient hook and exposes sanityClient on the 'sanity:client' module.”

In v1.x the global was the mechanism: the integration injected a page-SSR script that created the client and parked it on globalThis, and the public API was a hook that just read it back — which is also why the config “had to work or it throws”, since the injected createClient(config) ran on every SSR page load whether you used the client or not:
One surprise from reading the current source: the global assignment was never actually removed. Even the latest v3.5.0 still injects a back-compat shim on the server:
So yes — in the latest package the global exists purely for backward compatibility. Three things to be precise about:
It is the same client, not a second one.

The global is just another reference to the sanity:client singleton, so v1-era code that reads the global keeps working after an upgrade — consistent with the v2.0.0 changelog saying the old API was deprecated, not removed.
It is server-side only.
The page-ssr injection runs during server rendering, so the global exists in the Node/SSR runtime — it is not leaked into the browser bundle for visitors.
It is an undocumented shim, not an API.
The README only documents importing from 'sanity:client'. Do not write new code against the global — it could disappear in any major version.
It is not purely cosmetic.

The shim imports sanity:client on every SSR render, so createClient(config) executes whether you use the client or not — meaning “the config has to work or it throws” remains true on the latest version. Upgrading fixes the global-as-API; it does not remove the obligation to keep the integration's config valid. Removing the shim (and accepting a custom client via a module specifier) is something we can bring to engineering.

Practically: if the docs and API you are using say globalThis.sanityClient, you are on v1.x — upgrade past 2.0.0 (current is 3.5.0) and import from 'sanity:client' instead. If you merely noticed the global existing at runtime, that is expected even on latest; it is a lingering shim you never have to touch as an API.

question: Which version of @sanity/astro fixed the globalThis.sanityClient problem?

children.text: Option A — environment flag (how this repo started)
Run the server in one of two modes: plain
npm run dev
for published content, and
PUBLIC_SANITY_VISUAL_EDITING_ENABLED=true astro dev

for drafts + stega + overlays, with the client config keyed off import.meta.env at module level. About ten lines and fine for a first local bring-up — but it structurally cannot ship: a deployed preview-mode server serves drafts to the entire internet, editors cannot check the public view without a second server, and switching modes means restarting.
Option B — preview URL secret (what this site uses now)

One server, decided per request. The frontend cannot detect “this user is logged into Sanity” — the session lives on the Studio's origin — so the Studio proves itself: the Presentation tool opens the iframe through /api/preview/enable with a short-lived signed secret; the route validates it server-side with @sanity/preview-url-secret and sets an unforgeable preview cookie; middleware flips Astro.locals.preview; the data layer and the overlay script follow per request. Same trust model as next-sanity's draft mode, hand-rolled for Astro in about 80 lines.

question: How should preview mode work — an environment variable, or automatically per request?

children.text: The @sanity/astro integration builds its own client from serializable config and cannot accept an instance. Instead of maintaining a second client with duplicated config, invert the wrapping: derive your logging client from the integration-owned one.
The pattern
sanityClient.withConfig({...})
returns a cheap derived instance — one config source, one client lineage. Lint-ban direct sanity:client imports so only the wrapper circulates.

excerpt: Deriving your wrapped client from sanity:client via withConfig() keeps astro.config.mjs the single source of truth.
title: One client to rule them all

children.text: Yes — the app is standard SSR with no exotic APIs, and Astro's deployment story runs through adapters. This repo ships the Vercel adapter (@astrojs/vercel); for container platforms (ECS, Cloud Run, GKE) swap one line in astro.config.mjs to @astrojs/node ({ mode: 'standalone' }) and run node dist/server/entry.mjs in a ~10-line Dockerfile. AWS has no official adapter: use the container path or the community astro-sst adapter for Lambda. Cloudflare has an official adapter but Workers is not full Node. The one hard requirement everywhere: SSR per request — preview mode is decided per request by cookie, so the site cannot be statically exported.
Three portability fixes are baked into this codebase so serverless and container platforms behave identically:
Runtime secrets via astro:env.

Vite inlines import.meta.env.* values at build time, so a token injected only into the running environment (Vercel settings, k8s secrets, Cloud Run) would be undefined in the bundle and preview mode would silently disable. The token is declared with envField({ context: 'server', access: 'secret' }) and read at runtime instead — building without the token present still works.
Web Crypto HMAC instead of node:crypto.

The preview-cookie signature uses crypto.subtle.sign('HMAC', …), which runs identically on Node, Vercel, and edge/Workers runtimes (Cloudflare would otherwise need the nodejs_compat flag). Same hex output as the old createHmac version, so existing cookies stay valid.
Environment-driven cookie flags.
In production the Studio iframe is cross-origin over HTTPS, so the preview cookie is set with SameSite=None; Secure; on localhost dev over plain HTTP it falls back to Lax.

Deployment checklist for any platform: add the production domain to the Sanity project's CORS origins; point the Studio's presentationTool previewUrl.origin (and PUBLIC_SANITY_STUDIO_URL for stega) at the deployed URLs; and never edge-cache SSR HTML without varying on the sanity-preview cookie — cached preview responses must not leak to end users. The Studio itself deploys separately and statically anywhere (sanity deploy gives you *.sanity.studio for free).

children.text: Never trust remembered version numbers — check the registry before pinning:
npm view <pkg> version
for the latest release and
npm view <pkg> peerDependencies
for what it is allowed to sit next to.

This repo was first scaffolded with sanity@^4 and astro@^5 from stale memory while Astro 7, Sanity 6 and TypeScript 7 were current. Upgrading required zero source changes because the peer ranges allowed it — @sanity/astro supports astro ^2 through ^7 and sanity ^3.99 through ^6. Two gotchas surfaced: a clean install dropped a transitively-hoisted @types/node the typecheck had silently relied on (declare it explicitly), and package names are easy to conflate — sanity (the Studio, v6.x) and @sanity/client (v7.x) version independently.

question: How do we make sure we are on the latest package versions?

children.text: Mostly yes — but “optimistic” means something specific, so here is the honest latency ladder, worst to best:
Full reload
(the refresh handler; this repo's 'vanilla' flavor) — seconds; simplest possible wiring.
client.listen() / Live Content API re-fetch.

Event-driven: editor types → draft commits → listener fires → re-fetch and patch the DOM. A real round trip, so not optimistic — but drafts commit continuously as the editor types, so it feels near-live (sub-second). Plain vanilla JS.
Loaders over comlink

(this repo's 'svelte' flavor). @sanity/core-loader connects to the Presentation tool over postMessage; in preview, Presentation runs your queries against its local state — including uncommitted pending edits — and streams results into the iframe. Close-to-optimistic latency, no React. For a typical editing session this is hard to distinguish from the React experience.
useOptimistic (React-only).

Presentation pushes the pending mutation into the iframe before it is committed and the hook patches local React state immediately — zero network round trip. Needs client-side state to patch, which is why there is no vanilla equivalent. Its unique value in practice is mostly the drag-reorder UX, where the list moves during the drag.
One correction to an earlier claim: the history adapter does not help with edit latency at all — it syncs URLs and navigation between Presentation and the iframe.
Both approaches live in this codebase behind an env flag
PUBLIC_VISUAL_EDITING_FLAVOR=vanilla|svelte

(build-time). 'vanilla' is the plain script with reload-driven updates. 'svelte' mounts two islands in preview: a 10-line Svelte wrapper around enableVisualEditing(), and a live-query header component — inside Presentation the site title and description update as the editor types, no reload. Published visitors get zero preview code in either flavor.

Two implementation findings worth knowing: the first-party @sanity/visual-editing/svelte component and the @sanity/svelte-loader barrel both import $app/navigation, so they only build inside SvelteKit — in an Astro island, wrap the core enableVisualEditing() yourself (10 lines) and use @sanity/core-loader directly. And core-loader's stores are nanostores, which happen to satisfy the Svelte store contract, so $store auto-subscription works natively in Svelte components.

children.text: The error means the page inside the iframe is not running enableVisualEditing() — the message misleadingly points at setup when the setup is usually fine.

The specific trap we hit: in Astro 7 the dev server is a persistent daemon. Starting a different mode while a server is up silently attaches to the running one, so the preview environment flag never applies and the page serves published mode with no visual-editing script. Fix:
npx astro dev stop
before switching (this repo's npm dev script now guards it). With per-request preview the whole failure mode disappears — there is only one mode.
Works in Chrome but not Safari?

Safari blocks third-party cookies that are not partitioned. In production the Studio loads the site in a cross-site iframe, so the preview cookie set by the enable route counts as third-party and is silently dropped — Presentation reports “Unable to connect” and draft mode never activates, while the same setup works in Chrome. Fix: set the CHIPS Partitioned attribute on the cookie when the enable route is hit from a cross-site iframe, and expire both the partitioned and unpartitioned variants in the disable route (this site's routes do both; the official Visual Editing with Astro guide documents the same trap).

Also worth knowing: the wss://…api.sanity.io socket warning in the Studio console is a separate, usually transient listener issue (check VPN/proxy if it persists), and “No matching documents” in the side panel resolves once the connection is up. If it still fails, inspect the console inside the preview iframe itself.

children.text: No. The premise is right, but the conclusion is wrong. Step by step:
First, Svelte and SvelteKit are different things.

Svelte is the component framework. SvelteKit is a full meta-framework — a competitor to Astro, with its own router and server. You cannot run SvelteKit inside an Astro project, and you don't need to: Astro runs Svelte components directly via @astrojs/svelte, which an Astro + Svelte monorepo already has.
Second, the complaint is factually correct.

We verified it by building: both @sanity/visual-editing/svelte and @sanity/svelte-loader fail in an Astro project with “failed to resolve import ‘$app/navigation’” — a virtual module that only exists inside SvelteKit. Sanity's first-party Svelte tooling really is coupled to Kit.
Third, that does not mean React.
The Kit-only parts are thin wrappers around framework-agnostic cores. In Astro you use the cores directly, with your existing Svelte:

answer.code:
<script>
  import { onMount } from 'svelte'
  import { enableVisualEditing } from '@sanity/visual-editing'

  onMount(() => enableVisualEditing())
</script>

children.text: That is the whole replacement for the SvelteKit component — mount it as an island with client:only="svelte". For live-as-you-type preview queries, use @sanity/core-loader (the framework-agnostic layer the official loaders wrap): its stores are nanostores, which happen to satisfy the Svelte store contract, so $store syntax works in Svelte components with no adapter. Both are running in this site right now, with zero React in package.json — set PUBLIC_VISUAL_EDITING_FLAVOR=svelte and look.

So the corrected version of the complaint is: “The official Svelte tooling assumes SvelteKit, so it doesn't drop into Astro — but the core packages are framework-agnostic, so an Astro + Svelte monorepo needs a ten-line Svelte wrapper, not React.” The gap between those two sentences is the legitimate feature request: the Svelte support exists but is coupled to Kit's router when nothing about overlays requires it. Shipping an Astro-compatible Svelte export would close it.

question: The official Svelte tooling is SvelteKit-only — so do we have to bundle React into our Astro + Svelte monorepo?

children.text: Yes. A plain Astro
<script>

tag is bundled by Vite and runs in the browser with full access to window, document.cookie and postMessage. The browser-only-APIs justification is real — it appears verbatim in the official Visual Editing with Astro guide:

“The client:only=“react” directive is critical. It tells Astro to render these components exclusively on the client side using React, with no server-side rendering attempt. This is necessary because both components use browser-only APIs (window, document.cookie, postMessage).” —
Visual Editing with Astro, sanity.io/docs
Read precisely, that sentence justifies the
client:only

directive — why there is no SSR attempt — not the React requirement itself. The React requirement is justified elsewhere in the same guide: “react(): Required because the visual editing overlay components are React components that run in the browser” — which is circular (React is required because the components are React). A component touching window at render time cannot be server-rendered, so once you choose React it must be forced client-only; a plain script never server-renders, so the whole problem evaporates. Nothing about the browser APIs necessitates React — it is an implementation choice in the Sanity packages, not an Astro platform limitation.

@sanity/visual-editing
package ships a framework-agnostic entry point. A plain Astro script tag has full access to window, document.cookie, and postMessage — no React island required.
What the docs recommend vs what is required

The React requirement is an implementation choice of the official components, not an Astro platform limitation. This very page proves it: click any text in the Presentation tool and it opens the matching field.
Browser APIs work natively in Astro scripts; the only React left is inside Sanity's lazy-loaded preview overlay.
